segment:
She felt a sudden, strong sensation of being looked at.
“Hello.”
The greeting was low and quiet. It didn’t make her flinch; it wasn’t rude, just unexpected.
“Hi.”
The hand holding the glass had been resting on his knee. It curled casually around the rim and raised the glass to his mouth.
His hair fell into his eyes when he drank. He set the glass on the table, leaned forward and pulled the hair from his forehead, pushing it back into place with his fingers.
She saw the tattoo on the back of his hand then, a small triangle of green inside an even smaller black triangle.
“Do you live here, too?” she asked.
“No.” He shifted his position on the couch so that his feet lay flat against the opposite arm rest. “I’m going to Livia’s class tonight.”
He seemed perfectly at ease in his own space, but didn’t seem to feel obliged to make himself a comfortable space inside her head. She was momentarily uncomfortable with the imbalance.
“Oh? She doesn’t usually—” She stopped herself.
“Usually what?”
She shrugged and shifted the overnight bag to her other shoulder. “It’s unusual for people who live elsewhere to come just for classes.”
A look passed across his face, then vanished. He laughed suddenly, turning the laughter into a cough by covering his mouth. “Unusual, eh?”
“Unusual,” she said, nodding. She shifted again, searching for some position that felt less exposed than any other. “Why don’t you live here? The group rate makes it easier.”
He shrugged. She didn’t know why she was talking to him.
She was going to say good-bye.
But there was no reason to walk out of the room and leave him behind, was there? It didn’t make any sense for either of them to avoid being here. He could have left.
“I do have other interests,” he said, suddenly leaning forward. “It’s not like this place is the only one in the world.” He laughed again. “It would be pretty sad if it was.”
His face held no trace of humor; but his voice had a certain lightness she found disturbing.
He picked up his glass and drank some more of the cold liquid, then set it down on the table beside him and straightened his shoulders. His chest rose slightly as he took another deep breath.
text:
When Mara walked into the common room at six fifteen, someone was already there. Someone younger, it seemed.
She couldn’t make out the face behind the blond hair. But the body was fine enough, leaning back on the couch with bare legs crossed and arms flung in opposite directions, one palm pressing the padded wall and the other wrist resting on the low table beside him.
She stood stock-still by the doorway for a moment, aware of her breath and of his awareness that she was here. He stirred and tilted his head; a face turned toward her, expressionless.

segment:
She let out a small sound.
“I’m sorry to disturb you,” she said. “I didn’t mean to intrude.” She was about to take a step back when she noticed the book on the table: The Complete Works of William Blake. Not exactly a privacy warning sign.
She paused, trying to judge what he might want or need. Was he reading or sleeping? Waiting for someone else, maybe? Probably reading. He wasn’t wearing his glasses but his eyes were open. “I thought I could do a little writing in the study,” she added tentatively, “but the door’s locked. I was going to leave a note that says I’m here, but I don’t know what to say.”
“I thought it was locked because Adrian isn’t supposed to be in there,” the young man said absently. He put his hand behind his head, tilted back farther, and closed his eyes. She recognized him as Jonah, one of the other newcomers. His profile looked younger than when he was dressed up for the group meeting. “I mean, I guess it’s also to keep the rest of us out, in case we want to do something in there without Adrian’s permission.”
Mara’s mind ran back through her training and through what Adrian had said earlier. The idea that Adrian would let the other residents have free rein in their rooms had never even crossed her mind. Jonah was right, it didn’t make any sense; of course he wouldn’t do that. She felt a little self-conscious, realizing she’d assumed the worst on Adrian’s part. “Right, of course.”
“Do you want me to show you?”
Mara turned to the study door again. “Is it possible to open?” she said, mostly to herself. She put a hand on the handle. She moved away from it, unsure if that was really what she wanted. “I don’t know,” she answered. She looked at Jonah again. “Can you—could I—”
“Take a look?” His eyes were still closed and his head was still tilted back, but he moved a little and patted the cushion of the couch.
She took one last look out the hallway window at the green lawn, then let herself in. He reached for something on the coffee table and held it out to her.
“Here,” he said. “Heh, I wish he’d put something like this in the welcome packet.”

Then he raised his free arm slightly. A hand held a cigarette, one finger flicked the smoke in the air as he turned, then the hand dropped to rest on his thigh while he looked at her.
A quick glance showed a large paperback open on the table, words and pictures in squares and speech bubbles across the page, the comics of Mara’s youth, though she didn’t recognize the particular titles. He went back to his reading before she could get near enough to identify them.

“I’m Mara,” she said, pausing with her hand on the doorknob as he kept his eyes down on the book.
He half turned and looked at her with cool blue eyes, still reading. “Welcome.”
No other greeting, but he sat up, pulling his feet to one side and stretching the other arm out along the back of the couch. He gestured to indicate a spot beside him. “I’m Jonah.”

She went over and sat down on the sofa, turning to face him. She waited for another word of greeting or introduction, but he didn’t say anything else. He kept glancing up and looking at her in between moments of reading, but there was no visible response except for slight changes in expression, and he didn’t try to interact any further.
This wasn’t what Mara had expected, based on the brief and informal introductions that had taken place during orientation. There were three people living here now, the two men she had met in orientation and the woman who had arrived after dinner. Mara couldn’t quite remember names, but the two men were very friendly, and the woman seemed shy yet cheerful.
Mara’s first impression had been that everyone in the house got along well; they talked with each other and did things together, and seemed at ease with one another in a way that didn’t leave much room for newcomers.
When she had come into the dining room for dinner, Livia had welcomed her again and sat her next to a woman who hadn’t said a word to Mara since their first introduction that morning, even when Mara had tried to make small talk about orientation. The others were very friendly and welcoming, but this woman sat staring at Mara like she was an object instead of a person.
Now the others were out somewhere, and she was alone with Jonah.
